conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that regular vitamin C supplements do not meaningfully prevent colds in the general population, stating that routine supplementation solely to prevent colds is not supported by evidence.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** For most people, regular vitamin C supplements do **not meaningfully prevent getting colds**. A Cochrane review of 29 comparisons (11,306 participants) found no effect on cold incidence in the ordinary population. Therefore, routine high-dose vitamin C solely to prevent colds is not supported.

Regular use may produce a **small benefit once colds occur**: average duration was reduced about 8% in adults and 14% in children, with some reduction in symptom severity. This is not the same as preventing infection. Evidence suggests there may be exceptions for people undergoing brief, intense physical stress (for example, strenuous exercise or cold exposure), but that does not establish benefit for the general public.

High doses are not necessary for most people and can cause adverse effects; discuss supplements with a clinician if you have kidney disease, iron-overload conditions, take medications, or are considering large doses.

Sources:  
- Cochrane review: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold  
- Cochrane Library review: https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4/full  
- NCCIH summary: https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/the-common-cold-and-complementary-health-approaches
